payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make this look like a comic book photo
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Compared with the source, does the edited image visibly use comic-book visual styling?
node.criteria: Pass if the edited image has recognizable comic-book visual treatment absent from the source, such as visibly stylized contours or graphic color treatment; fail if that treatment is absent or only a grain/filter effect; unknown if the comparison is not observable.
node.source_quote: Make this look like a comic book photo
node.endpoint: The image visibly has comic-book visual styling.
node.necessity: The instruction explicitly requests a comic-book look; without visible comic-book styling, that requested transformation is incomplete.

node_traces.evidence: Compared with the source, the edited street scene retains ordinary photographic detail and muted colors. It shows no recognizable comic-book contours, halftone shading, or graphic color treatment; the visible change is mainly darker/grainier texture.

d2: The node checks only whether photographic appearance is retained, so it can pass even when the requested comic-book treatment is absent or too weak. The trace supports that narrow finding, but the reference label is aggregate and cannot establish that this individual criterion should fail. Keep the photographic-retention check, and clarify its scope so it is evaluated alongside a separate, explicit check for visible comic-book styling; do not make this node fail merely because it passes. The edited image appears to preserve the source’s photographic street scene with stronger contrast, but the trace does not identify concrete comic-book cues or assess whether the requested style is achieved. Ensure the decision distinguishes evidence for photographic appearance from evidence for the requested stylization, and use unknown when the images do not support a confident judgment. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is indicated.
